# A macro whose expansions no binding reaches is checked against its body

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `73b731e` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/equiv-unreachable-macro-sites`, made on
2026-11-14 after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Equivalence: its tests compare the Rust with the C.

## Signal

An agent had to work out a rule by hand that a skill should have stated. A translation batch
and then its review had to settle it, and the review's task message had to raise it.

## Evidence

`testing`'s Equivalence tests section compares a port with its C, and "a C function the raw
bindings do not reach, one with internal linkage, is compared through the functions that
call it". A header macro has no symbol, so the C can be run only where it expands, inside
the functions that expand it. When the raw bindings reach none of those functions, the
section says nothing about what stands in for the comparison.

- `wave-200/batch-0/run-1` ported `mac::MIN` (`deps/ntlmclient/compat.h`). Its only
  expansions are in `ntlm.c`'s static `des_key_from_password` and `generate_lm_hash`. These
  are reached only through `ntlm_client_response`, which the raw bindings do not declare
  (`grep ntlm_client sys/libgit2` finds nothing), and no suite reaches them (`ntlm.c` is at
  `0.00`% in every suite). The batch wrote no `equiv` test. Its six `unit_pub` tests check
  the function against the macro's replacement list, `(((x) < (y)) ? (x) : (y))`, at
  `ntlm.c`'s three sites, ties and unordered pairs. Its commit message argues the choice.
- Its module pass, `wave-200/batch-1/run-1`, was asked by its task message to "judge both
  against `porting-symbols`' Macros section and `testing`". It found no rule to judge them
  by. It accepted the batch's reading: an equivalence test needs a Rust side that
  translates the C it runs, and the functions that expand `MIN` have none until `ntlm.c` is
  ported. A test reaching them through new bindings would compare DES and OpenSSL, not the
  macro.
- `wave-225/batch-1/run-1` (`src/util/strnlen.h`) shows the other case. `p_strnlen`'s
  expansion in `git__strndup` is reached through `StrFree::dup_prefix`, so its `equiv`
  tests compare it there.

## Destination

The spec: `testing`'s Equivalence tests section, which the reviewer role evolves.

## Change

Append to the paragraph that ends "is compared through the functions that call it":

> A macro is compared where it expands, through the functions that hold its expansions.
> When the raw bindings reach none of them, no equivalence test compares it: its `unit_pub`
> tests check it against the replacement list at each expansion site's arguments, and the
> batch reports the sites as unreached, until the port of the module that holds them
> compares them.

Its record entry's recurrence signal: a task message, report or plan correction that settles
again what stands in for a macro's equivalence tests.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |

| a macro is compared where it expands; one whose expansion sites no raw binding reaches has no equivalence test, is checked by unit tests against its replacement list, and is reported as unreached until its sites' module is ported | `libgit2-crustify`, `equiv-unreachable-macro-sites` | crustify `73b731e` | four runs settled by hand what stands in for a macro's equivalence tests when the bindings reach none of its expansion sites | a task message, report or plan correction that settles again what stands in for a macro's equivalence tests | watched |

## Validation

The two batches above, read under the sentence. `wave-200/batch-0`'s tests and report meet
it as they stand: unit tests over the replacement list at `ntlm.c`'s sites, and the sites
reported unreached in its dashboard notes. `wave-225/batch-0` falls under the sentence's
first half and keeps its `equiv` tests. No run was repeated, since neither batch failed.

name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

  of Crustify;

- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or

  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies

would hold for any C codebase.

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

# Porting symbols

How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.

## 1. Functions

A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.

A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. The gateway checks each export against the raw binding of the C declaration
it replaces, as [`testing-gates`](../../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions
section asks, in a constant the compiler evaluates, `const _: () = { let _ = [sys::<name>,
<name>]; };`, whose two function items coerce to one function-pointer type only where their
signatures agree; the binding is allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it and its declaration in its
header, once no remaining C references it. C that only a configuration the target is built
without compiles, such as another platform's, is no remaining C: like a test case
configured out, as [`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Tests
follow their modules section describes, it holds no export back, and a build under that
configuration meets the function undeclared where it calls it.

A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,

goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C

forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as

expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

Functional equivalence defects in the workset's API that its equivalence tests missed,
while the C it translates exists: in a port, until the module's switch. A divergence is a defect only when it is unintended: a doc comment, a `CHANGELOG`

deliberate, and one that corrects a C defect on purpose is no finding.

### 3.5 Logic (`logic`)
## 5. Reproducers

A `ub`, `equiv` or `logic` candidate becomes a finding only once a reproducer proves it,
and so does a `contracts` candidate that claims a contract can be broken. A contract that merely
asks for more than the implementation needs, or a missing justification, is a finding
without one.

- A UB reproducer triggers one of the available sanitizers from Rust, and its report
  carries the sanitizer's trace. One targeting the safe public API carries
  `#[forbid(unsafe_code)]`; one targeting the unsafe API, or breaking a contract, honours
  the `# Safety` obligation. One reaching an export calls it as C would, through its raw
  binding, within the C declaration's contract.
- An equivalence reproducer fails one of [`testing`](../testing/SKILL.md)'s equivalence
  comparisons while running the raw C and the public Rust API, and its report carries the
  failing assertion. Once the C is gone, a behaviour finding is a `logic` one.
- A logic reproducer fails a Rust assertion of what the specification it cites requires,
  and its report carries the failing assertion.

Each reproducer is a standalone Cargo package: its `Cargo.toml` declares an empty
`[workspace]` table and depends on the affected crate through a relative `path`, and its
`src/main.rs` runs one scenario, so that running it exits non-zero on the affected commit.

## 6. Fixes

Under `fix`, every finding of the batch's objectives is patched:

- `unsafety`: the entry point is made safe;
- `contracts`: the `# Safety` obligation or `// SAFETY:` justification is corrected, or,
  when the contract can be broken, the code it guards, and the reproducer becomes a UB
  regression test;
- `ub`, `equiv` and `logic`: the defect is patched, and the reproducer becomes a
  regression test of the same kind, a UB test, an equivalence test or a unit test, on the
  side of the module it reaches. A UB
  regression test either runs without triggering a sanitizer, or fails to compile because
  the patch removed the safe path that reached the defect;
- `ergonomics`: the API is improved, and its consumers in the crate follow;
- `idiom`, `conventions` and `misc`: the transliteration, deviation or defect is fixed;

tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.

  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

region does.

name: evolution-record
description: "The record of the changes that landed in Crustify and its tools, `EVOLUTION.md`: its rows, their recurrence signals and statuses, when the watched rows are read, and how evolution itself evolves from the record. # Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

mac::MIN

The macro is the native fn min<T: PartialOrd>(x: T, y: T) -> T, its body
over any PartialOrd type: ties and unordered pairs return y, as the C's <

macro's C users are static functions of ntlm.c, which the raw bindings do
not reach. Proposal: macro-incidental-double-evaluation (porting-symbols).

**Verdict: rejected.** Two fixes are required, and the third finding below should be fixed too. Each is a few words. The change is otherwise sound: the evidence shows the signal, the change serves Equivalence, it sits in the right section and uses no target names, and its validation holds. The dashboard note for `wave-200/batch-0` does report the `ntlm.c` sites as reached by no suite. As you asked, I ran no gate or rerun.

## Does it weaken a check?

**As written, yes, in one reading. With fix 1 below, no.**

- **Why it can weaken one now.** The sentence just before the new text says a C function the raw bindings "do not reach" means one with internal linkage. Read with that meaning, "when the raw bindings reach none of them" exempts any macro whose expansions all sit in internal functions. That holds even when bound callers run those functions, where the old text would compare them through those callers.
- **A run already read it that way.** Batch 0's commit message (`4b6e5a4db`) gives its reason as "the macro's C users are static functions of ntlm.c, which the raw bindings do not reach". Only its dashboard note gives the caller-based reason.
- **What it does with that fixed.** It settles a case the old text left silent. The comparison is put off until the port of the module that holds the sites, not dropped. No gate, objective, lint or tool detection changes, and the record row needs no `weakens a check` mark.

## Fixes required

1. **"Reach" is used in two senses.** As described above, it can drop equivalence tests that the preceding sentence would still get through callers, and that weakening would go unseen.
